strengths: First benchmark to explicitly annotate auxiliary line construction methods, addressing a documented gap in existing geometry benchmarks
Comprehensive 5-dimensional evaluation framework with fine-grained metrics (ACS, PCS, PQS, auxiliary line impact, error types) substantially more sophisticated than existing approaches
Large-scale empirical study evaluating 13 diverse state-of-the-art MLLMs (7 thinking, 6 non-thinking models) across 2,186 authentic problems from 34 provincial regions
Authentic, high-quality dataset with expert curation, careful quality checks, and dual problem types (calculation/proving) at realistic difficulty levels

Useful empirical findings including quantification of performance degradation on long-step problems, identification of model "laziness" in proving, and demonstration of auxiliary line guidance benefits
Strong reproducibility effort with detailed appendices, hyperparameters, error analysis examples, ROUGE-L contamination analysis (2.28%-3.77%), and promised code/data release
weaknesses: Evaluator reliability not validated: uses newly released o4-mini without inter-rater agreement studies or manual verification; prior work cited but this specific evaluator choice lacks justification
Dataset annotation relies on automated Gemini-2.5-Pro for step segmentation and auxiliary line extraction without inter-annotator agreement metrics or manual verification
Reduced dataset scale for expensive models: GeoLaux-mini comprises only 330 problems (15% of full set) for o1 and o3, limiting generalizability of thinking model findings

Auxiliary line evaluation measures guided use of provided auxiliary lines rather than spontaneous construction, artificially inflating measured benefit and not directly testing auxiliary line discovery capability

Insufficient depth on key findings: 'laziness in proving' attributed to given conclusions but lacks detailed error analysis; long-step degradation is expected given known LLM limitations; limited actionable insights for improvement
Statistical rigor lacking: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars on main findings; limited variance analysis across problem types and step lengths

Limited technical novelty: individual metrics (ACS, PCS, error types) are standard; PQS weighting function choice (exponential form) and tanh scaling hyperparameter (α=3.5) lack principled justification
Generalization concerns: dataset limited to plane geometry from Chinese entrance exams; findings may not extend to other geometry domains, educational systems, or languages

Incomplete comparative analysis: limited interpretation of simple vs. complex auxiliary line performance differences (Figure 8); no analysis of problem characteristics predicting degradation; auxiliary line benefit not analyzed for non-thinking models
Presentation density: key findings reliant on figures (6, 7, 9) with minimal text interpretation; connection between evaluation framework and findings could be clearer
